transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doctor. Yeah, so... my job actually sent me. I do general maintenance and repair work, mostly for this big apartment complex across town. Which is usually fine, except the parking there is just an absolute nightmare. The other day I had to park three blocks away and lug my whole tool bag—the big heavy canvas one with the reinforced bottom—all the way to building C. My shoulder is still killing me from it. I keep telling myself I should probably get one of those rolling carts, but the wheels always get stuck in the gravel near the dumpsters anyway, so what's the point, you know? 

But, um... right, why I'm here. My supervisor, Dave, told me I had to come see someone. I just... I keep forgetting scheduled callbacks. And the work orders. Like, I'll promise a tenant I'm coming right back with a new air filter or a wrench, and then I just completely forget the basic follow-ups I promised people. It's just piled up so much lately. Dave actually sent me here because there's a lead tech spot opening up, and he said I'm gonna lose my shot at moving up if I don't get this sorted out.
Have you always had trouble remembering things and staying organized, or is this something that's gotten worse recently?

Well, I've probably always been a little scatterbrained, but it's definitely gotten noticeably worse recently. Like, for about the last 11 months? That's when the new management company took over and changed our whole department over to these digital work orders. They gave us all these cheap little tablets to carry around, and they want everything strictly documented on them now. 

And honestly, the glare on those screens when you're outside working on a condenser unit is just awful. I actually tried buying one of those anti-glare screen protectors online, but when I put it on, it got all these little dust bubbles trapped underneath. It drove me absolutely crazy. My niece usually puts those on for me because she has such a steady hand. She just went off to college for graphic design, actually, which is great, she's so artistic and I'm really proud of her... but yeah, without her around I just completely messed up the screen protector. 

Wait, what was I talking about? Oh, right. The new management. Yeah, since they switched us to the digital system and started demanding all this strict documentation 11 months ago, it's just been so much worse. I can't keep track of it all.
Over these past 11 months when your memory and organization got worse, have you noticed any changes in your mood—like feeling more sad, anxious, or just down in general?

Sad or down? No, I don't think so. I mean, I get frustrated with the work orders, sure, but not depressed or anything. 

Actually, speaking of anxious, there's this one tenant in building F—Mrs. Higgins—she is *always* anxious. She calls the emergency maintenance line every single time she hears a pipe creak. I went over there on Tuesday because she swore her radiator was leaking and ruining the hardwood, but it turned out it was just her cat knocking over its water bowl. That cat is massive, by the way. It's this big orange tabby named Marmalade, gotta be at least twenty pounds. I keep telling her she needs to put him on a diet, because he keeps breaking the window blinds trying to squeeze onto the sill. And management buys the absolute cheapest plastic blinds in bulk, so they just snap right down the middle the second any weight is on them, and then I'm the one who has to go string up a new set... 

Wait, sorry. What did you ask me? Oh, right, my mood. Yeah, no, I haven't been feeling sad or anxious myself. Just... scattered, I guess.

When you're working on a repair job that requires focus—like fixing an air conditioning unit or replacing a valve—do you find it hard to concentrate and stay on that one task, or do you do okay once you're actually working on something?

Well, the actual hands-on fixing part isn't usually the problem, if I can just get to it. But it's those digital work orders again. I can start one thinking I've got it, you know? Like I'm looking right at the screen, reading the notes for the job. But halfway through, my mind just... slips off. 

Like yesterday, I was trying to read this work order for a leaky faucet, and I heard this loud scraping noise from the parking lot. Turns out it was the garbage truck. They always come on Thursdays, but they used to come on Wednesdays before the city changed the routes. The driver, this guy named Sal, he always tries to back into this one narrow spot near the dumpsters, and he scrapes the side of the brick wall almost every time. I've had to patch that brickwork twice this year already. The mortar never quite matches because the original bricks have been fading in the sun for twenty years, and you just can't replicate that kind of weathering, you know? I even tried mixing a little bit of dirt into the mortar last time to make it look older, which actually worked okay, but it's still not perfect. 

Anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, the work orders. Yeah, so I'll hear a noise like the garbage truck, or I'll just start thinking about the next job I have to do, and then I look back at the tablet and realize I have absolutely no idea what I just read. I have to start all over again. It's like my brain just won't stay on the screen.

When you're sitting down trying to focus on something—like reading those work orders on the tablet—do you find yourself fidgeting a lot, tapping your fingers, bouncing your leg, or feeling like you just can't sit still? Or is it more that your mind wanders even though your body is calm?

No, I don't really do that. I'm not, you know, bouncing around or tapping my feet or anything. I can sit perfectly still. It's just my brain that won't stay put. 

Actually, speaking of sitting still, my sister's dog is the exact opposite. She has this little Jack Russell terrier mix named Buster, and I swear that dog vibrates. He literally cannot stop moving. She brought him over last weekend when we were doing a barbecue, and he spent the entire three hours just running laps around my patio furniture. He completely ruined my hostas. I spent all spring trying to get those hostas to come back after the frost we had in late April. Do you remember that frost? It was so weird for it to get that cold that late in the year. The news said it was some kind of freak polar vortex thing, but it completely wiped out my neighbor's tomato plants too. He was so mad because he started them from seeds indoors back in February. He's got this whole grow-light setup in his basement that must use so much electricity...

Wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, right, fidgeting. Yeah, no, I don't really fidget or anything. My body is fine, it's just my mind that keeps wandering off.

When you're at work or in your daily life, do you find yourself doing things without thinking them through first—like interrupting people, making quick decisions you later regret, or acting on impulses without considering the consequences?

No, I don't think I do that. I mean, I'm not the type to just blurt things out or jump into something without looking. I like to think things through, you know? 

Actually, speaking of jumping into things, my brother-in-law is terrible about that. He bought this old pontoon boat off Craigslist last summer without even looking at the motor. He just saw the price and thought it was a steal. Well, it turns out the whole steering cable was rusted solid, and the pontoons had these tiny pinhole leaks that you couldn't even see until you got it in the water. We took it out on the lake for the Fourth of July, and about an hour in, the left side started sitting noticeably lower than the right. We had to get towed back to the marina by this guy on a jet ski. And jet skis are so loud, aren't they? I don't understand how people can ride those things all day. The whine of the engine just echoes across the water and ruins the peace and quiet for everyone else trying to fish. My dad used to take me fishing when I was little, and he always said the most important part of fishing was being quiet so you didn't scare the fish. We'd sit out there for hours with just a couple of sandwiches...

Sorry, what was the question? Oh, acting on impulse. No, I don't really do that. I'm pretty cautious, honestly.

Have people around you—like your supervisor Dave, family members, or coworkers—ever mentioned that you seem restless, fidgety, or like you have trouble sitting still? Or has anyone said you seem like you're always on the go?

No, Dave hasn't said anything like that. Nobody has, really. Like I said, I'm not much of a fidgeter. I'm usually the one standing there quietly while everyone else is running around. 

Dave actually complains more about the younger guys, like Tommy. Tommy started a few months ago and he's always pacing around the break room, tossing his keys in the air and catching them. Drives Dave up the wall. Dave's got this thing about noise in the break room because he likes to read the newspaper on his lunch break. A real, physical newspaper, too. He gets the local paper delivered every morning. I didn't even know they still printed that one, to be honest. The ink always gets on his fingers, and then he goes and touches the white doorframes in the hallway. I'm the one who has to go around with the Magic Eraser once a month to clean off all these little gray fingerprints. Those Magic Erasers are amazing, though. They're just melamine foam, but they get scuff marks off the linoleum like nothing else. I buy them in bulk online because the name-brand ones at the hardware store are way too expensive. You can get a pack of a hundred for like ten bucks if you don't care about the packaging. I gave a bunch to my sister for her kitchen...

Wait, sorry. Did you ask about Dave? Yeah, he's never said I'm restless. Just that I take too long on the work orders.
Has anyone ever told you that you seem to have a lot of energy, or that you're always moving around or doing something, even if you don't feel like you're fidgeting?

No, not at all. If anything, they probably think I'm too quiet or just standing around too much. Nobody's ever accused me of having a lot of energy. 

Actually, speaking of energy, you know what has way too much energy? Those ridiculous drinks the younger guys at the shop bring in. Tommy—the guy I mentioned before—he drinks like three of those giant Monster energy cans before noon. I swear, I don't know how his heart doesn't just explode right out of his chest. And he leaves the empty cans everywhere. I'm always finding them on the workbenches, or shoved behind the drill press. I had to empty the shop's recycling bin on Tuesday, and the bottom of it was practically glued to the floor from all the sticky syrup leaking out of those things. We have this big blue bin that the city is supposed to pick up on Thursdays, but they just changed the collection route. Now the truck comes barreling down the alley behind the shop at like 5:15 in the morning. The backup beeper is so loud it echoes off the brick walls. It's exactly like the garbage truck that comes down my street at home, which wakes up my cat, Barnaby, every single time. He's a rescue, mostly tabby but with these huge white paws, and he absolutely hates loud noises. Whenever that truck comes by, he dives straight under my bed and won't come out until I shake his bag of treats...

Wait, sorry, I lost track again. What did you ask me? Oh, about people saying I have a lot of energy. Right. No, nobody says I'm always moving around or anything. I'm pretty stationary, really.

When you need to do something that has multiple steps—like planning out your day's work orders or organizing a bigger repair job—do you find it hard to figure out where to start or how to break it down into smaller pieces?

Yeah, I guess sometimes. I don't know, I just kind of look at the pile of work orders and... well, I don't really have a system. I just grab one. 

Though, speaking of work orders, they just changed the software we use to print them out. It used to be this really simple program, just black and white text, easy to read. Now they upgraded to this cloud-based thing that has all these color-coded tabs and drop-down menus. It's supposed to be more efficient, but the printer in the office is this ancient laser jet from like 2008, so it just prints all the colors in these weird, muddy shades of gray anyway. You can't even tell the difference between an "urgent" red tag and a "routine" green tag. I tried to tell the office manager, Brenda, that we needed a new printer if we were going to use this fancy software. But Brenda is always so worried about the budget. She won't even buy the good coffee for the break room anymore. We used to get the big tubs of Folgers, which isn't great, but it's coffee. Now she buys this generic store brand that comes in a plain white bag. It tastes like burnt dirt. I brought in my own French press last week just so I could have a decent cup in the morning. French presses are great, but cleaning the grounds out is such a pain. You can't dump them down the sink or they'll clog the pipes, and if you scrape them into the trash, they make the whole bag heavy and wet...

Sorry, what was the question? Planning out the work orders? Yeah, I don't know. I just kind of take them as they come, I guess. I don't really sit down and plan it all out.

During the day, do you find yourself feeling unusually tired or sleepy, even when you've had enough sleep the night before? Like, do you ever struggle to keep your eyes open or feel like you're fighting to stay awake while you're working?

No, I don't really get sleepy like that. I mean, I'm awake. I don't struggle to keep my eyes open or anything. I'm usually pretty alert, just... you know, doing whatever. 

Although, speaking of sleep, my neighbor's dog has been keeping me up a bit lately. It's this little terrier mix, cute but it barks at absolutely everything. A leaf blows across the driveway? Barking. The mail carrier comes by? Barking. And they leave him out in the yard until like eleven at night. I tried talking to them about it, but they just said he's "expressing himself." I don't even know what that means for a dog. It's not like he's painting a picture. My cat, Barnaby—the one I told you about with the white paws—he just sits in the window and glares at the dog. Barnaby is so quiet. The only time he makes noise is when he wants his wet food. He gets half a can of the chicken and liver pate every evening at exactly 6:00 PM. If I'm even five minutes late, he starts doing this little trill sound and rubbing against my legs. I have to buy it at this specific pet store across town because the grocery store only carries the seafood flavors, and Barnaby refuses to eat fish. It's so funny, right? A cat that hates fish. But the pet store is right next to this amazing bakery that makes these huge blueberry muffins. I usually grab one when I go to get the cat food. The muffins have that coarse sugar sprinkled on top, which gives it this great crunch...

Wait, sorry. Sleepy during the day? No, I don't have that problem. I'm fine staying awake.
Do you find yourself falling asleep during the day without meaning to—like nodding off while sitting down, or having trouble staying awake even when you're trying to focus on something?

No, I don't fall asleep like that. I'm not nodding off in the middle of things. 

Although, finding a place to sit down and actually nod off at the shop would be a miracle anyway. Brenda—the office manager I mentioned earlier—she finally replaced the chairs in the break room, but she bought these rigid plastic ones from some discount supply catalog. They're bright orange. She said they'd brighten the space up, but they are so incredibly uncomfortable you can't sit in them for more than five minutes without your back aching. Tommy actually tried leaning back in one last week and one of the back legs just completely snapped off. He went tumbling backward right into the vending machine. 

Which, by the way, that vending machine is a total scam. The coil on the D4 slot, where they keep the peanut butter crackers, is bent. So if you try to buy them, they just get stuck halfway and dangle there. You end up having to buy a heavy bag of almonds from the slot directly above it just to knock the crackers down. I tried to tell the vendor about it the last time he came to restock, but he was this young kid wearing huge noise-canceling headphones the whole time, just nodding his head to whatever music he was listening to. I don't even think he heard a single word I said. People just walk around in their own little bubbles now, you know? My nephew is exactly the same way, always staring at his phone when he comes over for dinner. Last Thanksgiving I made this huge turkey, and I swear he didn't look up from his screen once while he was eating... 

Oh, wait, I'm doing it again. You asked if I was nodding off during the day. Right. No, definitely not. I don't fall asleep during the day at all.

You mentioned that when you're actually doing the hands-on repair work—like fixing a faucet or an air conditioning unit—you can focus okay. But with the digital work orders on the tablet, your mind just slips off. Is it that you can concentrate fine when you're doing physical work with your hands, but you really struggle to pay attention to reading and paperwork specifically?

Yeah, that's pretty much it. When my hands are busy, I'm good. But with the tablet... I can start a digital work order thinking I’ve got it, I'm ready to go. But then halfway through reading the notes, my mind just completely slips off to the next noise in the shop or whatever the next job on the list is. 

Like yesterday, there was this loud clanking coming from the bay next to mine. Tommy was trying to fix the suspension on this old golf cart the property managers use to get around the complex. I don't know why they don't just buy a new one, that thing is basically held together by duct tape and prayers at this point. Anyway, Tommy dropped his wrench, and it echoed everywhere. He has this massive new tool chest he got from Harbor Freight, the bright red one with like twenty drawers. I told him he didn't need one that big, but he insisted. He's always buying gadgets he doesn't need. Like last month he bought this magnetic wristband thing that's supposed to hold your screws while you work? He wore it once, and it just kept getting stuck to the metal framing of the doors we were fixing. It was hilarious, he looked like he was handcuffed to the doorjamb. I laughed so hard I spilled my coffee, which reminds me, I still need to get some of that heavy-duty cleaner to get the stain out of my work boots. They're those composite toe ones, super comfortable, way lighter than steel toe, but the leather stains really easily if you're not careful...

Sorry, I completely lost my train of thought. What were we talking about? Oh, the reading and the paperwork. Right. Yeah, my mind just slips off to a noise or whatever, and then I look back down at the tablet and realize I have absolutely no idea what I just looked at. I'll have "read" the whole paragraph but I couldn't tell you a single word of it.

When you're reading something that really interests you—like instructions for a repair technique, or maybe a hobby you enjoy—can you sit down and read through the whole thing without your mind wandering, or does your attention slip away even with stuff you actually care about?

Honestly, it’s exactly like what I just told you about those digital work orders. Even if it’s something I really care about, it doesn't seem to matter. I’ll sit down, pull up an article or a guide, thinking, 'Okay, I've got this, I'm super interested.' But halfway through, my mind just slips off to the next noise outside or whatever project I want to do next, and I realize I don't know what I just looked at. 

Like, I'm really into restoring vintage lamps right now. It's a fun hobby. I found this gorgeous Art Deco desk lamp at the swap meet on Sunday. The guy running the table wanted fifty bucks, which was crazy because the wiring was totally shot and the brass was completely oxidized green. I talked him down to twenty. He was selling out of the back of this wild 1970s conversion van, the kind with the wood paneling and the orange shag carpet on the walls and ceiling. I haven't seen one of those in decades. My cousin Joey used to drive one exactly like it when we were younger, except his had a giant airbrushed wizard on the side of it. We used to take it down to the lake every summer, and Joey would always bring this huge cooler full of those little foil-wrapped sandwiches... 

Oh, wait. Sorry. We were talking about reading. Right. Yeah, so even if I'm reading a step-by-step tutorial on how to rewire that exact lamp, and I really want to learn how to do it, my attention still just completely slips away. I'll read a whole page and realize I wasn't actually taking any of it in.

When someone is talking to you—like Dave giving you instructions, or a tenant explaining what's wrong with their apartment—can you listen and follow along okay, or does your mind wander during conversations the same way it does when you're reading?

Yeah, it happens with talking, too. Like, when my supervisor, Dave, talks straight to me about a repair we need to do, or one of the upcoming property audits, I’ll be looking right at him. 

But speaking of audits, Dave gets so incredibly worked up about them. The regional managers come down from corporate, and they always wear these ridiculous suits. Last month, this guy showed up in a grey three-piece suit to inspect the main boiler room. A boiler room! It was like ninety degrees down there, and he was just sweating right through his fancy silk tie. Which, honestly, serves him right, because those corporate guys have no idea what it actually takes to keep this complex running. They just look at spreadsheets. Dave is terrified of them, though, which is funny because he's this big, burly guy who drives an ancient Volvo station wagon. You know, the really boxy ones from the nineties? It’s got like three hundred thousand miles on it, and the fabric on the ceiling of the car is completely sagging down so it touches your hair when you sit in it. He tried to pin it up with thumbtacks, but they keep falling out, and I told him one of these days he's going to sit on one and...

Wait, sorry. I'm doing it again, aren't I? You were asking about listening to people. Right. 

So, like I was saying, when Dave is talking to me about a job, I am looking right at him, making eye contact and everything. But only the first part of what he says actually sticks in my head. The rest of it just completely disappears, and I end up having to ask him to say it all over again.

When Dave is giving you those instructions and you ask him to repeat himself, does he seem frustrated or annoyed that you didn't catch it the first time? Like, does this happen a lot with him or other people?

Oh, yeah, he gets super frustrated. I mean, like I was just saying, I'll be looking right at him while he's talking straight to me about a repair or one of those audits, and only the first part actually sticks in my brain. Then I have to ask him to say it all over again, and you can just see his face get a little red. 

He already has high blood pressure, I'm pretty sure. He's always chewing on those giant bottles of chalky antacid tablets. He buys them in bulk from Costco. Man, I love Costco, but you go in there for paper towels and you come out with a kayak and a fifty-pound bag of dog food. Last time I went, they had these really nice heavy-duty outdoor string lights on sale. I bought three boxes to put up on my back patio, but I haven't gotten around to hanging them yet because my ladder at home is too short. I keep meaning to borrow the tall aluminum one from the main maintenance shed here. The latch on that shed is super tricky, though. You have to pull the door towards you and jiggle the key at the exact same time, otherwise it won't budge. I told management we need to replace it, but they never want to spend the money on the little things...

Wait, what was I talking about? Oh, Dave getting annoyed. Right. 

Yeah, it happens all the time, with him and with the tenants, too. It's just exactly like I said—I'm staring right at them, looking them dead in the eye, and only the very beginning of what they say registers. The rest just vanishes, and I have to make them repeat the whole thing. Dave usually just sighs really loud and rubs his temples before he starts over, but yeah, I know it drives him crazy.

You mentioned that even when you're reading something you really care about—like those lamp restoration tutorials—your mind still wanders halfway through. But I'm curious: when you're reading something that's really engaging and fast-paced, like a news story or a comic book or something that just grabs your attention immediately, does your mind still wander the same way, or is it different?

Well, even with fast-paced stuff like the news, it doesn't really change. Like, I get those breaking news alerts on my phone all the time. Just yesterday there was this big alert about a water main break over on 4th street. It completely flooded the basement of that old Italian restaurant, Sal's. Have you been to Sal's? They make this incredible baked ziti. Sal's wife, Maria, makes all the pasta by hand in the back. She's been doing it for like thirty years. She has arthritis now, though, so she wears these copper compression gloves. I bought a pair of those gloves for my elbows because swinging a hammer all day really takes it out of your joints, especially when you're working overhead. I had to patch a massive hole in the drywall ceiling in unit 4B last week because the upstairs tenant let their bathtub overflow, and my arm was just absolutely killing me by the end of the day... 

Wait, what were you asking? Oh, reading fast stuff like the news. Right. 

Yeah, no, it doesn't matter if it's a quick, exciting news story or a comic or whatever. Honestly, it always goes right back to what I was saying earlier about my digital work orders. It's the exact same feeling. I can start a work order thinking, 'Okay, I’ve got it,' but halfway through reading the notes, my mind just slips off to the next noise in the hallway, or I start thinking about the next job I have to get to. Then I get to the bottom of the screen and realize I don’t know what I just looked at.

When you're doing the actual hands-on repair work—like physically fixing that faucet or working on the air conditioning unit—do you ever lose track of what step you're on, or do you pretty much stay focused on the physical task in front of you the whole time you're doing it?

Well, the physical part of the fixing, like actually turning the wrench on a faucet or wiring the AC, I usually stay pretty focused on that. Because my hands are busy, you know? Like last Tuesday, I was fixing this leaky P-trap under a bathroom sink in unit 3C. 

The tenant in 3C, Mrs. Higgins, she collects these little porcelain frogs. I mean, hundreds of them. They are everywhere in that bathroom. Lined up on the back of the toilet, around the tub, all over the vanity. You can barely put a tool down without knocking one over. I actually did knock one over a few months ago, this little green guy holding a tiny umbrella. I felt so incredibly bad, I took it back to my workshop to superglue it before she noticed. Superglue is so tricky, though, isn't it? If you don't wear gloves, you end up with your fingers stuck together for days. I tried using nail polish remover to get it off my skin once, but it just made my hands smell awful. My dog absolutely hated the smell. He wouldn't even let me pet him. He's a rescue, part beagle, part who-knows-what, and his nose is just so sensitive to chemicals... 

Wait, sorry. I'm drifting off again. You asked about losing track of steps during a repair. Right. 

So, like I was saying, the actual hands-on fixing part is usually fine. I don't really lose track while my hands are physically in the pipes or the wires. But it's the follow-through that gets me every time. I’ll begin a maintenance job, do the actual fix so everything is working perfectly, and then somehow I just leave the last steps completely undone. Like, I'll walk away without closing the ticket out on my tablet, or I'll forget to label the breaker panel I just rewired, or I won't even check back with the tenant to tell them the water is back on. It's like once the physical problem is solved, my brain decides the whole thing is over, and I just move on without actually finishing the job.

When you finish the actual repair work and the physical problem is solved, what typically happens next? Like, do you just naturally remember to go back and finish the paperwork, or do you have to force yourself to do it, or does it just completely slip your mind until Dave reminds you?

Oh, it completely slips my mind. Like, completely. I'll finish up, throw my wrenches in my bag, and just walk away. My toolbag is actually falling apart, now that I think about it. The zipper on the main pocket busted off like three months ago. I tried fixing it with a pair of needle-nose pliers, but the teeth on those heavy-duty zippers are just impossible to realign once they get bent. I really should just buy a new one. They have those nice canvas ones at Home Depot with the hard plastic bottoms so they don't get soaked if you set them down in a puddle. Puddles are a nightmare in the basement of building C, by the way. The drainage down there is awful, especially when it rains heavy in the spring. Last spring, we had a huge storm and I had to wade through ankle-deep water just to reach the sump pump. I ruined my favorite pair of work boots that day... 

Wait, sorry, what was I saying? Oh, right, the paperwork and forgetting things after the job. 

Yeah, I don't naturally remember any of it. Honestly, that's exactly what brought me in to see you today. I just keep forgetting scheduled callbacks, closing out the work orders, and even doing the basic follow-ups I promised the tenants. It’s piled up so much lately that work actually sent me here. They told me I need to get a handle on this before I completely lose my shot at moving up to a senior maintenance position.

When you finish a repair and the physical problem is fixed, do you feel like you just don't think about the paperwork or follow-up at all, or do you actually think about it but then somehow don't get around to doing it?

I'm not really sure, to be honest. It's hard to tell. Maybe it's a little of both? Like, I might have a split second where I think about grabbing my tablet as I'm walking back to the maintenance cart. 

But the cart is always such a mess, you know? I share it with Gary, and he just leaves his empty energy drink cans everywhere. He drinks those massive white Monster cans. I don't know how his heart handles it, honestly. My brother used to drink a ton of caffeine when he was driving long-haul trucks, and he ended up with terrible acid reflux. He had to completely change his diet, cut out tomatoes, coffee, everything. It was really tough on him because our family makes a lot of red sauce. My mom's recipe uses pork neck bones to flavor the gravy, which sounds kind of weird if you're not used to it, but it makes it so incredibly rich. She used to simmer it on the stove for like six hours every Sunday...

Wait, sorry, I lost track again. You were asking if I think about the paperwork or just don't think about it at all. 

Yeah, I really don't know. Once the wrench is down and the leak is stopped, my brain is just immediately on the next thing. I couldn't tell you if the thought to do the paperwork even crosses my mind before it's gone, or if it just never registers in the first place. It just doesn't happen.
